papers.title: The cellular neighbourhoods of adult gliomas and their clinical associations
papers.label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.24.26368523 v1

summary.one_liner: A single-cell spatial transcriptomic atlas of 275 adult glioma patients (2.6 million cells) reports recurrent cellular neighbourhoods across glioma types, with some neighbourhood abundances linked to survival in astrocytoma.
summary.plain: This study looks at the most common malignant brain tumours in adults, gliomas, and asks whether the different types of cells inside them are arranged in repeating local groups. The researchers mapped the position and activity of about 2.6 million cells from 275 patients, using a technique that measures which genes are switched on in each cell while keeping its location in the tissue. They found recurring cell "neighbourhoods" with particular immune and support-cell mixes, some shared across tumour types and some linked to clinical features.
summary.why: It suggests that the spatial layout of tumour cells, not only their molecular type, may carry information about prognosis, and the authors report that in astrocytoma neighbourhood abundance was associated with survival independently of WHO grade. Whether this could guide treatment or diagnosis is not shown in the text and would need further study.
summary.background:
- Gliomas are tumours arising from glial cells, the support cells of the brain; glioblastoma is the most aggressive common type.
- IDH mutations and 1p/19q codeletion are genetic markers used to classify these tumours.
- WHO grade is a standard pathology scale of how aggressive a tumour looks under the microscope.
- Single-cell spatial transcriptomics measures gene activity in individual cells while retaining their positions in a tissue slice.
- A "neighbourhood" here means a recurring group of nearby cells with a characteristic mix of cell types.
- AC-like (astrocyte-like) refers to a cell state resembling normal astrocytes, a type of glial cell.
- H&E is the routine stain used to view tissue sections under a microscope.
- Multiplexed protein imaging labels many proteins at once in the same tissue section.

papers.abstract: Glial tumours are the most common primary malignant brain tumours in adults and comprise molecularly and histologically distinct entities with diverse outcomes. Despite this diversity, they arise within a shared anatomical environment, suggesting that common organisational principles may shape tumour heterogeneity. However, how cellular states are organised across gliomas and whether this organisation relates to clinical outcomes remains unclear. To that end, we generated a single-cell resolution spatial transcriptomic atlas of 2.6 million cells from 275 patients spanning IDH-wildtype glioblastoma, IDH-mutant and chromosome 1p/19q codeleted oligodendroglioma, IDH-mutant astrocytoma and ependymoma. Across diagnoses, we show how heterogeneous tumour cell states are spatially organised into recurrent neighbourhoods with distinct immune and glial composition, which in turn assemble into a higher-order architecture. Among these cellular neighbourhoods, some, such as the astrocyte-like (AC-like), are conserved across entities, whereas others segregate by clinicopathological parameters. AI-powered histopathology further reveals selective association of neighbourhoods within histological clusters, providing a link between molecular spatial organisation to routine H&E morphology. In astrocytoma, neighbourhood abundance is associated with patient survival independently of WHO grade, with AC-like enrichment linked to favourable outcomes. Same-cell high-plex spatial transcriptomics and multiplexed protein imaging in an independent astrocytoma cohort validated these neighbourhoods and further confirmed enrichment of oligodendrocytes within the TBI neighbourhood. Collectively, our findings reveal that glial tumours are spatially encoded through recurrent multicellular neighbourhoods across different molecular entities, showing clinical relevance beyond conventional histology and providing a foundation for analogous investigation across cancer types.

papers.title: Integrated real-world and translational studies nominate CREB binding protein/EP3001 inhibition to overcome androgen receptor pathway modulator resistance in men with prostate cancer
papers.label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.24.26368506 v1

summary.one_liner: Regulatory network models built from multi-omic data of over 10,000 prostate cancer patients point to EP300/CBP as a target in androgen pathway modulator-resistant disease, supported by preclinical work with the inhibitor pocenbrodib and one clinical case.
summary.plain: Prostate cancer drugs that block male hormone signalling often stop working over time, and doctors need new targets for these resistant tumours. The authors used computer models of gene regulation, built from large sets of patient molecular data, to find a protein called EP300 (and its close relative CBP) linked to resistance. They then tested a new inhibitor of these proteins, pocenbrodib, in lab and animal studies, and report benefit in one patient.
summary.why: Resistance to hormone-blocking drugs is nearly universal in advanced prostate cancer, so a new candidate target is of interest. The evidence is limited: the human benefit rests on a single patient, so the finding is a lead for further testing rather than an established treatment.
summary.background:
- Androgen pathway modulators (APMs): drugs that block male hormones such as testosterone from driving prostate cancer growth through the androgen receptor.
- Therapy resistance: when tumours keep growing despite treatment.
- Multi-omic data: measurements across several layers of biology (genes, proteins, and so on) from the same patients.
- Regulatory network model: a computer map of which genes and proteins control others.
- EP300 / CBP: related proteins that switch genes on by adding chemical tags (acetylation) to histones and other proteins.
- Acetylomics: measuring these acetyl tags across the proteome.
- Oxidative phosphorylation and fatty acid metabolism: cell processes that produce energy; the paper links the drug to suppressing them.
- In vitro / in vivo: lab-dish and living-animal experiments; a single-patient clinical report is far weaker evidence than a trial.

papers.abstract: Androgen pathway modulators (APMs) have significantly improved outcomes for men with metastatic prostate cancer, but the evolution of therapy resistance is nearly universal, and there remains a major clinical need to identify actionable vulnerabilities for therapy-resistant disease. To address this need, we employed regulatory network models that leverage multi-omic data from over 10,000 prostate cancer patients with longitudinal clinical data. Analysis of the architecture of the network models identified EP300 as the top actionable target associated with androgen receptor-mediated therapy resistance. These observations were validated using a novel inhibitor of CBP/EP300, pocenbrodib, which showed preclinical activity in vitro and in vivo. Acetylomics analysis and functional studies pinpointed inhibition of oxidative phosphorylation and fatty acid metabolism as key mechanisms of action for pocenbrodib. Clinical benefit for this agent was demonstrated in a patient with metastatic APM-resistant prostate cancer (NCT04575766), highlighting CBP/EP300 as a key target for further translation.

papers.title: Beyond standardized health-related quality of life measures: Additional symptoms and problems reported through the EORTC WISP instrument in the EUonQoL-Kit study across European cancer populations
papers.label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.23.26368179 v1

summary.background:
- Health-related quality of life (HRQoL): how a illness and its treatment affect daily physical, emotional and social wellbeing, usually measured by questionnaire.
- Patient-reported outcomes (PROs): symptoms and experiences reported directly by patients rather than by clinicians.
- EUonQoL-Kit: a toolkit developed with many stakeholders to inform health policy across Europe, combining standard closed questions with an open-ended section.
- EORTC WISP: an open-ended instrument from the European Organisation for Research and Treatment of Cancer where patients write in up to three symptoms or problems.
- Three groups studied: patients in active treatment, cancer survivors, and patients in palliative (comfort-focused) care.
- Descriptive study: it reports patterns and comparisons, not cause and effect. The text reports that differences between groups in the common additional symptoms were not statistically significant, while some subgroup differences in who responded were.
summary.one_liner: A descriptive analysis of open-ended "write in three symptoms/problems" (EORTC WISP) responses from a 32-country European validation study of the EUonQoL-Kit, examining which additional symptoms patients raised beyond standardized quality-of-life items and how this differed across patients in treatment, survivors, and palliative care.
summary.plain: Standard questionnaires about quality of life in cancer ask about a fixed list of symptoms, so they can miss things that matter to a particular patient. This study looked at a free-text section where people could name up to three other problems they had. About 12% of the 4,284 participants wrote in problems, and roughly 40% of the 954 written items were not covered by the fixed questions.
summary.why: The findings suggest that an open-ended question could be added to a European cancer quality-of-life toolkit to catch concerns the fixed questions miss, without making the questionnaire longer for everyone. Whether this improves care or policy decisions is not shown in the text.

papers.abstract: Background: Standardized health-related quality of life (HRQoL) measures may not capture all symptoms/problems relevant to people with cancer. The European Oncology Quality of Life toolkit (EUonQoL-Kit), co-created with multiple stakeholders to inform health policy across Europe, combines standardized closed-ended patient-reported outcome (PRO) items with the European Organisation for Research and Treatment of Cancer (EORTC) open-ended Write In three Symptoms/Problems (WISP) instrument. We aimed to identify symptoms/problems reported via WISP beyond the EUonQoL-Kit, examine differences in background characteristics between WISP respondents and non-respondents, and compare additional symptom/problem reporting across three target cancer populations: patients in active treatment, survivors, and patients in palliative care. Methodology: This descriptive analysis used data from adults with current or previous cancer diagnoses participating in a multicenter validation study across 32 European countries (22 August 2024 - 7 July 2025). WISP responses were categorized, and subsequently their prevalence and severity were calculated. Participant characteristics and the ten most frequently reported additional symptoms/problems were compared across groups using t-tests, chi-square tests, or Fisher's exact tests, as appropriate. Results: Among 4,284 included participants, 519 (12.1%) reported 954 symptoms/problems on WISP, of which 383 (40.1%) were not covered by EUonQoL-Kit v2 closed-ended items. Women, participants from Western and Northern Europe, highly educated and those diagnosed with breast cancer were more likely to respond to the WISP than other subgroups (all p < 0.05). No statistically significant differences were found in the prevalence of common additional symptoms/problems (p [≥] 0.130). Descriptively, numbness/tingling, skin problems and bleeding were most reported by patients in active treatment; indigestion, incontinence, and vision problems in survivors; and edema, cough and itching in palliative care. Conclusions: The EORTC WISP complemented standardized PRO assessment by capturing additional symptoms/problems. Integrating open-ended WISP reporting into the final toolkit may enhance HRQoL assessment across European cancer populations while identifying population-specific concerns without expanding predefined items for all respondents.

papers.title: Aneuploidy and structural genome complexity beyond the EWSR1 fusion is associated with evolution and outcome in clear cell sarcoma
authors: Tavares, L. S. P. D. S.
papers.label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.20.26368414 v1

summary.background:
- Clear cell sarcoma: an ultra-rare soft-tissue cancer, usually defined by a fusion of two genes (EWSR1 and a CREB-family gene).
- Gene fusion: an abnormal joining of parts of two genes, often driving cancer growth.
- Aneuploidy: having an abnormal number of whole chromosomes or chromosome pieces.
- Chromothripsis and chromoplexy: sudden, large-scale chromosome shattering and rearrangement events.
- Chromosomal instability: a tendency for chromosomes to be gained or lost repeatedly as cells divide.
- Subclonal diversification: the tumour splitting into genetically distinct sub-populations over time.
- MYC: a master growth-control gene; MGA normally restrains it.
- Ribosome biogenesis: the cell's manufacture of protein-building machinery, which fast-growing cancers often ramp up.
- Hazard of death: a statistical measure of risk of death at any given time, here compared between groups.
summary.one_liner: Multi-omic profiling of clear cell sarcoma tumours and cell lines shows extra genomic complexity beyond the defining EWSR1-CREB fusion, and links aneuploidy, chromosomal instability, 17q gain, 9p21.3 loss and TERT alteration to poorer survival and a MYC-driven ribosome biogenesis signature.
summary.plain: Clear cell sarcoma is a very rare cancer whose outcomes range from slow-growing to resistant to chemotherapy, even though the tumours share the same core genetic change. This study examined primary, recurrent and metastatic tumours and cell lines using several layers of genetic and gene-activity data. The authors report that these tumours carry additional structural damage to chromosomes beyond the main fusion, and that the extent of these changes is linked to how the disease evolves and how patients fare.
summary.why: The work tries to explain why tumours with the same defining mutation behave so differently, and it proposes a possible molecular risk framework at diagnosis and a potential therapeutic target. Because the cancer is ultra-rare and the cohort details are not given in the text, these links should be treated as candidate findings that need independent confirmation.

papers.abstract: Clear cell sarcoma (CCS) is an ultra-rare cancer defined by EWSR1-CREB gene family fusions with clinical outcomes that range from indolent to chemotherapy-refractory metastatic disease. Through multi-omic profiling of primary, recurrent and metastatic tumours and cell lines, we show that CCS is more genomically complex than previously recognised. Beyond the fusion, tumours acquire chromoplexy, chromothripsis and an intermediate aneuploidy burden, with ongoing subclonal diversification. Recurrent events include chromosome17q gain and inactivation of the MYC antagonist MGA. Enriched transcriptional signatures of chromosomal instability,17q gain, 9p21.3 loss and TERT alteration each double the hazard of death, supporting a new molecular based CCS risk stratification framework at diagnosis. Transcriptomes converge on a MYC-driven ribosome biogenesis programme, a previously unrecognised therapeutic vulnerability. These findings address a central paradox of CCS, a shared oncogenic identity with divergent clinical fate, implicating tolerated aneuploidy and chromosomal diversification as candidate determinants of progression.

papers.title: Panel-agnostic tumour-only diagnosis of mismatch repair deficiency
papers.label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.19.26368513 v1

summary.background:
- Mismatch repair (MMR) is a cell system that fixes copying errors in DNA; when it fails (MMRd), mutations pile up.
- MMRd tumours can respond to immune checkpoint immunotherapy, so detecting them matters clinically.
- Standard confirmatory tests are immunohistochemistry (IHC, staining for repair proteins) and MSI-PCR (checking microsatellite instability, i.e. length changes in repeated DNA stretches).
- Targeted panels sequence only selected genes; tumour-only means no matched healthy-tissue sample is sequenced for comparison.
- Mutational signatures are characteristic patterns of mutation types that reveal the processes that caused them.
- Sensitivity is the share of true cases detected; specificity is the share of true non-cases correctly cleared.
summary.one_liner: A tumour-only classifier (captureMMRd) that infers mismatch repair deficiency from mutational signatures in somatic variant calls already produced by targeted panels, validated across 7,514 samples from 16 cohorts against IHC and MSI-PCR reference tests.
summary.plain: Some cancers lose a DNA repair system called mismatch repair, and patients whose tumours have this loss may respond to immunotherapy. Current tests for it often need a matched normal sample or special genetic markers that many routine gene panels lack. This paper describes an open-source tool that spots the loss using patterns in the mutations already found in a tumour's sequencing data.
summary.why: If it holds up, it could let hospitals that already run tumour-only gene panels screen for a treatment-relevant condition without adding a new test. The text reports strong agreement with standard lab tests, but these are retrospective results across many cohorts, and real-world performance on individual panels still needs checking.

papers.abstract: A diagnosis of mismatch repair deficiency (MMRd) can unlock immunotherapy treatment for a patient. However, existing sequencing-based detection methods require matched normal samples, panel-specific baselines or dedicated microsatellite loci, none of which are available to the tumour-only targeted panels that dominate routine clinical practice. Here we present captureMMRd, an open-source classifier that diagnoses MMRd using mutational signatures computed from the somatic variant calls any panel already produces. Applying a single locked model to 7,514 samples from 16 independent cohorts, spanning whole-exome, whole-genome, targeted panel and plasma cfDNA sequencing, captureMMRd achieved a pooled sensitivity of 94.36% and specificity of 99.02% against orthogonal MMR IHC and MSI-PCR testing, and outperformed microsatellite-based callers on panels with limited microsatellite content. We demonstrate that as few as 3 indels and 44 single-base substitutions are sufficient for reliable diagnosis, defining a minimum panel footprint that most clinically deployed assays already exceed. Our findings extend clinically actionable MMRd detection to the sequencing workflows of routine precision oncology, with the potential to broaden patient access to immunotherapy without new assays, baselines or matched normal samples.

papers.title: Baseline Prognosis and Treatment Benefit From First-Line Immunotherapy Strategies: Target Trial Emulations Across Advanced Solid Tumors
papers.label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.20.26368610 v1

summary.background:
- Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) are drugs that release the brakes on the immune system; pembrolizumab and nivolumab are examples.
- Chemotherapy and targeted therapy (e.g., BRAF/MEK inhibitors) are the main alternatives compared here.
- Target trial emulation: analyzing observational records as if they were a randomized trial, to reduce bias.
- Flatiron Health: a US electronic health record database of oncology patients.
- PD-L1 CPS/TPS, dMMR/MSI-H: tumor biomarkers used to predict who responds to immunotherapy.
- Restricted mean survival time (RMST): the average survival time over a fixed window (here 2 years), a way to compare groups.
- Overlap weighting and pseudo-observation regression: statistical methods for balancing groups and modeling survival.
- Interaction P value: tests whether the treatment effect differs across levels of a factor such as predicted prognosis.
summary.one_liner: A target trial emulation using US electronic health records (8,688 patients, first-line therapy 2011–2023) tests whether benefit from immunotherapy-based regimens varies with machine-learning-predicted 6-month baseline survival across five advanced solid tumor comparisons.
summary.plain: Doctors must choose first-line treatment for patients with advanced cancer, and some immunotherapy drugs cause early deaths in trials, especially in frail patients who are often given immunotherapy alone because it seems gentler. This study used real-world hospital records from the US to copy the design of trials and asked whether patients with a worse outlook gain more from adding chemotherapy than from immunotherapy alone. In head and neck, urothelial (bladder-lining), and possibly lung cancers, the answer was that patients with poorer predicted survival appeared to benefit more from chemotherapy-containing regimens, while in colorectal cancer and melanoma immunotherapy helped across the range of predicted prognosis.
summary.why: Trials rarely enroll the sickest patients, so this suggests baseline prognosis could guide treatment choice alongside tumor biomarkers. It is observational data, so the gradients are associations that may be affected by unmeasured differences between patients; the lung cancer result was not clearly significant.

papers.abstract: Background In randomized trials, first-line immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI)-based therapy has shown excess early mortality versus chemotherapy- or targeted therapy-containing regimens. ICI monotherapy is often chosen for frail patients because it is perceived as less toxic. Whether treatment benefit varies with baseline prognosis is unknown, as poor-prognosis patients are underrepresented in trials. Methods Using the US Flatiron Health electronic health record-derived database, we emulated target trials among 8,688 patients initiating first-line therapy during 2011-2023 across five comparisons: pembrolizumab plus chemotherapy versus pembrolizumab in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC; PD-L1 CPS [≥] 1 or unknown) and non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC; PD-L1 TPS [≥] 50%); carboplatin plus gemcitabine versus pembrolizumab in urothelial carcinoma; pembrolizumab versus chemotherapy in dMMR/MSI-H colorectal cancer; and ipilimumab plus nivolumab versus BRAF/MEK inhibition in BRAF-mutant melanoma. Baseline prognosis was estimated with machine learning models predicting 6-month survival. Overlap-weighted pseudo-observation regression evaluated whether differences in 2-year restricted mean survival time (RMST) varied with predicted survival. Results In HNSCC, adding chemotherapy to pembrolizumab did not clearly improve RMST overall (11.5 days; 95% CI, -18.4 to 41.1), but benefit was 102.4 days greater at the 10th versus 90th percentile of predicted survival (95% CI, 40.5 to 164.3; interaction P=.001). Similar gradients favored carboplatin plus gemcitabine over pembrolizumab in urothelial carcinoma (10th-90th percentile difference, 51.4 days; 95% CI, 4.8 to 98.1; P=.03) and, less certainly, adding chemotherapy to pembrolizumab in NSCLC (73.7 days; 95% CI, -3.7 to 151.2; P=.06). Higher-risk patients in these cohorts were more often trial-ineligible. ICI-based therapy improved overall RMST in colorectal cancer (difference, 79.7 days; 95% CI, 49.5 to 107.0) and melanoma (68.3 days; 95% CI, 33.9 to 101.9), without clear variation by predicted survival (interaction P=.32 and P=.91). Conclusions Among patients with poorer prognosis, chemotherapy-containing regimens were associated with greater benefit than ICI monotherapy in HNSCC and urothelial carcinoma, and possibly NSCLC. ICI-based therapy appeared beneficial across prognosis in dMMR/MSI-H colorectal cancer and BRAF-mutant melanoma. Baseline prognosis may complement tumor biomarkers when selecting first-line immunotherapy strategies.

papers.title: LCatlas: A Point-Of-Care Tool for Predicting Immunotherapy Outcomes in Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer
papers.label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.18.26368446 v1

summary.background:
- NSCLC: non-small cell lung cancer, the most common type of lung cancer.
- Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs): drugs that release the brakes on the immune system so it attacks tumours; "first-line" means the first treatment given.
- PD-L1 staining: a lab test on tumour tissue measuring a protein that affects immune response; higher levels often predict better response.
- Albumin, hemoglobin, lymphocytes, neutrophils, platelets: routine blood measures reflecting nutrition, oxygen-carrying capacity and immune status.
- AUC: area under the ROC curve, a 0–100% score of how well a model separates responders from non-responders (50% is chance).
- Sensitivity and specificity: the share of true responders correctly flagged, and the share of non-responders correctly flagged.
- Logistic regression, XGBoost, TabTransformer: three ways to build prediction models, from simple statistics to machine learning to an AI model for tabular data.
- Cross-validation: testing a model by repeatedly holding out parts of the same dataset; it is less convincing than testing on fully new patients.
summary.one_liner: A small retrospective study (79 first-line immunotherapy NSCLC patients) that builds LCatlas, a web tool using nine routine blood, clinical and molecular variables to predict response to first-line immunotherapy with or without chemotherapy, comparing logistic regression, XGBoost and TabTransformer models.
summary.plain: Lung cancer treatment with immune-boosting drugs works well for only some patients, and doctors currently lack an easy way to predict who will benefit. The authors built a free web tool, LCatlas, that takes nine details already in medical records (such as blood counts, albumin, smoking history and where the cancer has spread) and estimates the chance of a good response. In a small group of 79 patients, the tool's predictions were moderately accurate, and it was also tested on 28 other people.
summary.why: Predicting who benefits from expensive, sometimes toxic immunotherapy could help guide treatment choices if it holds up. However, the study is small, the accuracy figures come from cross-validation within the same 79 patients, and the claim of outperforming earlier studies, including deep-learning ones, rests on the authors' own comparison, so it needs external validation before clinical use.

papers.abstract: Non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) remains a leading cause of cancer mortality, with a minority of patients experiencing durable responses to first-line immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs). Currently, there are no easily accessible tools to predict clinical benefit to first-line immunotherapy. To address this gap, we developed LCatlas (https://www.lcatlas.org), a point-of-care web application designed to predict immunotherapy outcomes and inform evidence-based treatment decisions. Using data from 79 NSCLC patients receiving first-line immunotherapy, we extracted demographic, clinical, and molecular features from electronic medical records and compared three independent approaches, statistical model (logistic regression), machine learning (XGboost), and AI model (TabTransformer) to identify the most effective predictor. LCatlas accepts nine variables, gender, smoking history, bone/pleura/liver metastasis, PDL1 tumor staining, albumin level, hemoglobin level, lymphocyte count, neutrophil count, and platelet count, to predict responses to both immunotherapy and immunotherapy plus chemotherapy. LCatlas cross-validation yielded an area under the curve (AUC) of 79% [72% - 85%], with sensitivity of 87% [72% - 95%] and specificity of 78% [64% - 89%], outperforming previous studies including high-volume data-driven deep-learning approaches. In a validation cohort consisting of 28 individuals, it demonstrated a prediction accuracy of 82%. LCatlas may serve as a valuable point-of-care tool by identifying patients likely to experience extended immunotherapy or combination therapy using readily available medical data. Its evidence-based approach can optimize personalized treatment planning and thereby promote quality and safety of care.

papers.title: CIRCULATING IMMUNE DYNAMICS DURING NEOADJUVANT CHEMOIMMUNOTHERAPY IN EARLY TRIPLE-NEGATIVE BREAST CANCER
papers.label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.19.26368490 v1

summary.background:
- Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC): a subtype lacking the hormone and HER2 receptors that common targeted drugs act on, so it is treated largely with chemotherapy and immunotherapy.
- Neoadjuvant therapy: treatment given before surgery; pathological complete response (pCR) means no invasive cancer is seen in the removed tissue afterward.
- Pembrolizumab: an immune checkpoint inhibitor that releases the brakes on the immune system so it can attack tumor cells.
- Flow cytometry: a lab method that counts and sorts individual cells by surface markers.
- Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq): measures which genes are active in each individual cell.
- Pseudo-bulk analysis: averages single-cell data within each patient to compare patients rather than cells.
- CD38, IgM/IgD, CX3CR1, XBP1: cell-surface or internal molecular markers used to label immune cell types and states.
- False discovery rate (q value) and AUC: statistical measures of how likely a result is a chance finding and how well a marker separates two groups.
summary.one_liner: In 64 early triple-negative breast cancer patients given pembrolizumab-based neoadjuvant chemoimmunotherapy, baseline single-cell RNA profiling and serial flow cytometry of blood immune cells were used to nominate circulating signals (inflammatory pathway enrichment, a CX3CR1 CD4 memory signal, and CD38-defined B-cell dynamics) associated with pathological complete response.
summary.plain: Some breast cancer patients have all visible tumor removed by surgery after pre-operative drug treatment, and this "complete response" tends to predict better outcomes. This study looked at immune cells in the blood of 64 patients with a hard-to-treat breast cancer subtype to see whether patterns in those cells differ between patients who did and did not achieve complete response. The authors report several candidate patterns, but these are exploratory findings that still need confirmation in future studies.
summary.why: If confirmed, blood-based markers could help doctors anticipate who responds to immunotherapy without waiting for surgery, which is a real clinical need. The text presents these as candidate biomarkers only; several results are borderline after multiple-comparison correction (q values near 0.06 to 0.07), so they should be treated as hypotheses rather than established predictors.

papers.abstract: Background: Pathological complete response (pCR) after pembrolizumab-based neoadjuvant chemoimmunotherapy predicts improved outcomes in early triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC), but circulating immune determinants of response remain poorly characterized. Methods: The study included 64 patients with early TNBC treated with pembrolizumab-based neoadjuvant chemoimmunotherapy. Flow cytometry analyzed 125 peripheral-blood specimens collected at baseline, during treatment and before surgery. Baseline PBMCs from 22 patients underwent scRNA-seq, generating 135,271 quality-controlled cells. Analyses used nonparametric tests, effect sizes, FDR correction and sensitivity analyses. Results: Baseline scRNA-seq identified response-associated transcriptional differences. Patient-level pseudo-bulk analysis revealed enrichment of TNF-alpha/NF-kappaB signaling in cytotoxic T/NK and B cells from non-pCR patients (global q<=3.94e-7), together with MYC targets and mTORC1 signaling in cytotoxic T/NK cells (both global q=7.00e-5). T-cell analyses suggested preserved naive/memory features in pCR, while a higher proportion of CX3CR1-expressing cells within the CD4 memory/activation-like compartment was associated with pCR (q=0.0157; AUC=0.949). In B cells, pCR was associated with a nominally higher naive-like program score (P=0.029; q=0.059), supported by higher IGHM and IGHD signals, whereas XBP1 was higher in non-pCR. Flow cytometry identified treatment-associated B-cell remodeling. At pre-surgery, switched-memory B-cell CD38 balance was higher in pCR than non-pCR patients (62.6% versus 50.0%; P=0.0086; q=0.0667; Cliff's delta=0.651; AUC=0.825) and remained nominally significant in leave-one-patient-out analyses. Early increases in unswitched-memory B-cell CD38 balance were numerically greater in non-pCR patients, whereas pre-surgery switched-memory B-cell CD38 balance was higher in pCR patients. Conclusions: Baseline inflammatory and metabolic pathway enrichment was associated with non-pCR, whereas pCR-associated T-cell findings included a CD4 memory/activation-associated CX3CR1 signal and trends towards preserved naive/memory features. Together with time- and compartment-dependent B-cell remodeling, these findings nominate circulating transcriptional states and CD38-defined B-cell dynamics for prospective validation as candidate biomarkers of pathological response.

papers.title: Transcriptomic and Genomic Sequencing of South African Colorectal Cancer Patients Reveal Population-Specific Insights and Variants
papers.label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.19.26368287 v1

summary.background:
- Colorectal cancer: cancer of the colon or rectum (the large bowel).
- RNA sequencing: measures which genes are switched on and how strongly in a tissue sample.
- Whole-genome sequencing: reads the full DNA of a sample to find genetic variants (changes).
- Differentially expressed genes: genes that are more or less active in tumour than in normal tissue.
- Sensitivity / specificity / PPV / NPV: measures of how well a marker separates cancer from normal tissue.
- Consensus Molecular Subtypes (CMS): a classification of colorectal tumours into four groups based on gene activity patterns.
- APC mutation: a change in the APC gene, common in bowel cancer and an early driver of it.
- TCGA and Kaplan-Meier analysis: a public cancer genome database and a method for comparing survival over time.
summary.one_liner: Bulk RNA sequencing of 32 and whole-genome sequencing of 12 South African colorectal cancer samples identifies candidate diagnostic genes, tumour subtype distribution, APC mutation rates and novel variants in an underrepresented population.
summary.plain: Bowel cancer genetics have mostly been studied in people of European descent, so less is known about patients in Africa. This study sequenced the genes and their activity in tumour and healthy tissue from South African bowel cancer patients. It reports several genes that could help tell tumour from normal tissue, a different spread of tumour subtypes than in European studies, and some gene changes not previously linked to this cancer.
summary.why: Genetic studies that leave out African populations may miss biology and treatment targets that matter there, so this adds data to a gap. The text is a small study (32 and 12 samples), so the findings are best seen as leads for larger work rather than settled results; the link to a gut-brain axis is described by the authors as an emerging area and is not established by these data.

papers.abstract: Colorectal cancer (CRC) genomic studies have largely underrepresented African populations, limiting understanding of disease biology in these groups. This study addressed this gap by generating integrated genomic and transcriptomic data from South African (SA) CRC patients, establishing a foundation for future cancer studies. Bulk RNA sequencing of 32 samples identified several differentially expressed genes between tumour and normal samples, with AGAP3, AMPD2, ANKRD10, and SALL4 showing strong diagnostic performance (average sensitivity 99.9%, specificity 94.22%, PPV 99.9%, NPV 89.5%). SALL4 performed best and was validated using TCGA data and Kaplan-Meier survival analysis. Consensus Molecular Subtype classification revealed a distinct distribution, with enrichment of metabolic (CMS3, 30%) and mesenchymal (CMS4, 30%) subtypes and under-representation of canonical CMS2 (21%). APC mutation rates were lower than in European patients (~55% vs ~75%). Functional analysis identified inflammatory pathways as primary drivers of carcinogenesis, with viral influences exacerbating the inflammatory tumour microenvironment. Altered neural pathways in tumour samples suggested a consequential gut-brain axis loop as cancer infiltrates enervated tissue, an increasingly relevant field to which these data contribute. Whole-genome sequencing of 12 samples revealed pathogenic and likely pathogenic variants with transcriptomic differential expression; SMPD1, PERM1, PRRT2, and RP1 emerged as potential multi-omics markers, while novel mutations (KDM6A, C2CD2, TAF2, SLC6A16, OR5M10, PITRM1, TRIM64B, CARD11) were identified as previously unrecognised contributors to CRC progression in African samples. These findings expand genomic resources for African cancer research and provide new insights into the molecular landscape and tumourigenesis mechanisms of CRC in SA patients, supporting the development of population-specific precision oncology approaches.

papers.title: # Treatment- and tissue-context-specific isotope labeling patterns in patient-derived lung cancer tissues: an independent reanalysis of public metabolomics data
papers.label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.15.26368161 v1

summary.background:
- Patient-derived tissue: tissue taken from patients and kept alive in a dish or slice culture.
- Stable isotope tracing: feeding cells sugars or amino acids containing heavy, non-radioactive atoms (such as carbon-13) to follow how they are used in metabolism.
- Metabolomics: measuring many small chemical molecules in a sample.
- Pembrolizumab: an immunotherapy drug that blocks the PD-1 immune checkpoint.
- Beta-glucan (WGP): a fungal sugar polymer that can stimulate immune cells.
- P value: the probability of seeing a result at least this extreme if there were no real effect.
- Exact randomization test: a test that checks every possible way of assigning samples to groups, rather than relying on model assumptions.
- Benjamini-Hochberg q value: an adjustment that controls the share of false positives when many tests are run.
- Hedges' g: a standardized size-of-effect measure that corrects for small samples.
summary.one_liner: An independent reanalysis of a public isotope-tracing metabolomics dataset from small patient-derived lung cancer tissue cultures, testing how pembrolizumab and a beta-glucan treatment change labeling patterns, with exact randomization tests and multiple-comparison correction.
summary.plain: Researchers took a publicly shared set of lab measurements from lung tumor tissue slices grown outside the body and checked the analysis again from scratch. The tissue was fed sugar and amino acids tagged with a heavy carbon or nitrogen isotope, so scientists could follow where those atoms went inside cell chemistry. The reanalysis found the same general direction of effects as the original study, but with much weaker statistical support.
summary.why: It is a useful example of how small patient-derived experiments can produce effects that look more certain in standard model-based p values than they are under stricter tests. The authors describe the results as hypothesis-generating only, and the text does not show any link to clinical outcomes.

papers.abstract: Publicly deposited stable-isotope-resolved metabolomics data can be reanalyzed independently, but small patient-derived experiments may produce treatment effects with limited statistical resolution. We reanalyzed a public isotope-resolved metabolomics dataset from patient-derived lung cancer tissue cultures to quantify treatment- and tissue-specific labeling patterns and their uncertainty. We used 38 tissue samples from two patients: matched tumor and non-tumor slices from UK131 treated with vehicle or pembrolizumab and traced with U-13C6-glucose or U-13C5,15N2-glutamine (n = 3 per cell), and a pembrolizumab x WGP {beta}-glucan factorial experiment in UK2035 tumor tissue (n = 3/3/3/2). We recomputed protein-normalized pools, isotopologue distributions, atom-percent excess and pathway summaries. Effects were estimated with log2-scale linear models, Hedges' g, and exact randomization tests that enumerated all assignments compatible with each design; Benjamini-Hochberg q values were calculated within endpoint families. Sixteen macrophage samples were examined only descriptively. In UK131 tumor tissue, labeled non-oxidative pentose phosphate pathway intermediates increased 1.84-fold (model P = 0.036; exact tumor P = 0.10; exact interaction P = 0.16; q = 0.32). Weighted isotopic scrambling increased 1.31-fold (exact interaction P = 0.04; q = 0.20), and glutamine-derived glutathione diversion increased 1.66-fold (exact interaction P = 0.09; q = 0.22). In UK2035, the combination increased the labeled IMP/(ATP+GTP+UTP) ratio 3.64-fold (model interaction P = 3.2 x 10-4; exact P = 0.016; q = 0.097). No endpoint survived Benjamini-Hochberg correction at q < 0.05 in the exact analyses. The reanalysis reproduced the direction of the source study's principal labeling patterns but showed that their statistical support is weaker than model-based P values imply. These results should be treated as hypothesis-generating estimates for larger patient-derived studies, not as evidence of a validated metabolic bottleneck.

papers.title: CONSORTiUM-IO: A Phase 1 Study Evaluating VE800 Plus Nivolumab in Treatment of Select Refractory or Metastatic Cancers
papers.label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.13.26368051 v1

summary.one_liner: A first-in-human phase 1 trial testing VE800, a defined 11-strain commensal bacterial consortium, combined with nivolumab (anti-PD-1) in PD-1-refractory melanoma, PD-1-naive gastric/GEJ adenocarcinoma, and PD-1-naive MSS colorectal cancer, reporting good safety but no clear efficacy gain over historical rates.
summary.plain:
Researchers tested whether a standardized mix of 11 beneficial gut bacteria, given alongside an immunotherapy drug called nivolumab, could help patients with several hard-to-treat cancers. The combination was found to be well tolerated, but it did not do better than response rates seen in earlier studies. In patients with melanoma, those whose bodies picked up the added bacteria tended to have longer progression-free survival, meaning their disease stayed controlled for longer.</plain>
<parameter name="why">Gut bacteria are being studied as a way to make cancer immunotherapy work better, and this trial suggests a defined, lab-grown bacterial mix may be safer and more consistent than transplanted stool. The honest takeaway is that the main efficacy result was negative, and the link between bacterial engraftment and survival is only an exploratory finding from a small melanoma group.</why>
<parameter name="background">- Immunotherapy with anti-PD-1 drugs (such as nivolumab) works by releasing the brakes on the immune system so it can attack tumors.
- Gut microbiome: the community of bacteria living in the intestine, which can influence immune responses.
- Fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT): transferring stool from a donor to a patient; it is variable and carries infection risk.
- VE800: a defined consortium of 11 commensal bacterial strains grown from clonal cell banks, so each batch is intended to be the same.
- Engraftment: whether the added bacterial strains take hold and persist in the patient's gut.
- Phase 1 trial: an early study focused mainly on safety and dosing, with efficacy results only preliminary.
- Progression-free survival (PFS): time until the cancer grows or the patient dies.
- MSS colorectal cancer: microsatellite-stable tumors, which usually respond poorly to PD-1 drugs.</background>
<parameter name="difficulty">intermediate

papers.abstract: Microbiome modulation can augment responses to immunotherapy in advanced cancer. Early studies of anti-PD-1 therapies in combination with fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) reported efficacy in immunotherapy-naive and -refractory settings. However, FMTs are variable in composition, difficult to scale, and risk the transfer of emerging pathogens. VE800 is a consortium of 11 strains of commensal bacteria derived from healthy donors and grown from clonal cell banks. VE800 increased anti-PD-1 efficacy in preclinical models of cancer. CONSORTiUM-IO was a first-in-human, open-label phase 1 study that evaluated safety and efficacy of VE800 with nivolumab in advanced PD-1-refractory melanoma, PD-1-naive gastric/gastroesophageal junction (G/GEJ) adenocarcinoma and PD-1-naive microsatellite-stable colorectal cancer (MSS CRC). VE800 plus nivolumab was well tolerated but offered no improvement over historic response rates. Exploratory analyses in patients with melanoma revealed that VE800 strain engraftment was associated with greater progression-free survival (PFS) and increased immune activation peripherally. STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCEThe first-in-human study of the safety and efficacy of a defined bacterial consortium in combination with anti-PD-1 treatment in various solid tumors demonstrated the safety of the combination, albeit with low clinical efficacy. The results provide important knowledge and considerations about microbiome modulation in cancer, to help design future trials.

papers.title: Feasibility and Psychological Outcomes of a Clinical Meditation Intervention for Patients with Cancer: A Mixed-Methods Pilot Study
papers.label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.11.26367801 v1

summary.background:
- Psychological care (support for distress, anxiety, low mood) is a recognized part of cancer care.
- Mindfulness-based interventions (MBIs) are structured programs teaching attention-focused meditation; they are widely studied in cancer.
- Clinical Meditation is a Japanese method that combines traditional Buddhist meditation with a medical-care perspective.
- Pilot study: a small preliminary test to check whether a program is feasible before a larger trial.
- Single-arm: all participants receive the intervention; there is no comparison group.
- Mixed-methods: combines questionnaire scores with participants' written comments, analyzed for common themes.
- Friedman and Wilcoxon signed-rank tests: statistical tests for comparing repeated measurements in the same people; "adjusted P" means values corrected for testing several outcomes.
- Posttraumatic growth: positive personal change reported after a serious illness or stressful event.
- Attrition: only 8 of 11 completed the final assessment, and analyses used even smaller subsets.
summary.one_liner: A single-arm, mixed-methods pilot of an 8-week Clinical Meditation (Rinsho Meiso-ho) program for patients receiving pharmacotherapy for cancer, reporting feasibility, practice adherence, exploratory changes in spiritual well-being and posttraumatic growth, and thematic participant accounts.
summary.plain: Cancer patients often experience worry, low mood, and emotional strain during treatment, and meditation programs are sometimes offered to help. This small study tested whether a Japanese-developed meditation method, Clinical Meditation, could be run and accepted by 11 patients undergoing drug treatment over eight weeks. Most participants stayed in the program and reported feeling more spiritual well-being and personal growth at the midpoint and end, while practice frequency dropped in the second month and no change was seen in anxiety, depression, sleep, or fatigue.
summary.why: Meditation-based programs are already part of supportive cancer care in many countries, so knowing whether a different method is workable and acceptable adds to that evidence base. The study is too small and has no control group, so its outcome findings are only exploratory and should not be read as proof of benefit.

papers.abstract: BackgroundPsychological care is an important component of cancer care, addressing psychological distress and supporting patients as they cope with illness. Meditation-based approaches, including mindfulness-based interventions (MBIs), have been incorporated into supportive cancer care internationally. Clinical Meditation (Rinsho Meiso-ho), a meditation method developed in Japan, integrates traditional Buddhist meditation with a contemporary medical care perspective. However, its feasibility and psychological outcomes in patients with cancer have not been sufficiently studied. ObjectiveThis study aimed to evaluate the feasibility of a Clinical Meditation intervention and to explore psychological outcomes and participants experiences among patients with cancer who were receiving or scheduled to receive pharmacotherapy at the time of recruitment. MethodsThis single-arm pilot study used a convergent mixed-methods design to evaluate an 8-week program consisting of a 4-week structured phase (1 face-to-face session and 3 brief online group sessions, with prescribed home practice) and a 4-week self-directed phase (1 individual online session, with voluntary home practice). Feasibility was assessed descriptively using retention, attendance, practice frequency, and poststudy feedback. Anxiety, depression, insomnia, fatigue, spiritual well-being (SWB), and posttraumatic growth (PTG) were assessed at baseline, 4 weeks, and 8 weeks. Changes were examined using Friedman tests and exact Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, with adjustment for multiple comparisons. Free-text responses were analyzed thematically and integrated with questionnaire findings at the participant level. ResultsEleven patients were enrolled; 9 (81.8%) completed the 4-week assessment and 8 (72.7%) completed the 8-week assessment. Median practice frequency declined from 5-6 days per week during the structured first month to 3-4 days per week during the self-directed second month (P=.031). Quantitative analyses included 9 participants, of whom 8 completed all 3 assessments; qualitative analyses included 8 participants. SWB and PTG showed significant overall changes (adjusted P=.02 and P=.04, respectively). SWB was higher than baseline at 4 weeks (adjusted P=.012), but the difference was not significant at 8 weeks. PTG was higher than baseline at both 4 and 8 weeks (both adjusted P=.047). No significant changes were observed in anxiety, depression, insomnia, or fatigue. Five themes were identified, encompassing experiences such as relaxation, greater distance from rumination, and meditation as a source of support. Participants accounts generally aligned with increases in SWB and PTG scores, although perceived benefits did not always correspond to changes in all questionnaire measures. ConclusionsThis mixed-methods pilot study suggests that Clinical Meditation may be feasible and acceptable for patients with cancer, although sustaining meditation practice remains challenging. Exploratory increases in SWB and PTG warrant further investigation. Larger controlled studies, comparisons with established MBIs, and deeper qualitative research are needed to evaluate outcomes and clarify the distinctive features of Clinical Meditation.

papers.title: Updated outcome of patients with lung only osteosarcoma recurrence following surgical resection enrolled in phase 2 clinical trials: A report from the Children's Oncology Group
papers.label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.13.26368045 v1

summary.background:
- Osteosarcoma: a rare cancer of bone, mostly affecting adolescents and young adults.
- Recurrence: the cancer returning after initial treatment; here, returning only in the lungs and after surgical removal.
- Phase 2 trial: an early-stage study testing whether a treatment works, often with a single group rather than a comparison group.
- Single-arm trial: all patients get the same treatment, so results are compared with historical data rather than a concurrent control group.
- Event-free survival (EFS): time until cancer returns, progresses, or the patient dies.
- Overall survival (OS): time until death from any cause.
- Median: the midpoint of the time-to-event data; 95% confidence interval (CI): the range within which the true value likely falls.
- Randomization: assigning patients to treatment groups by chance, which allows fairer comparisons of effect size.
summary.one_liner: A pooled analysis of 99 patients from three Children's Oncology Group phase 2 single-arm trials updates survival benchmarks (event-free and overall survival) for osteosarcoma that returns only to the lungs after surgical removal, and examines which baseline factors affect outcome.
summary.plain: Osteosarcoma is a rare bone cancer that can come back in the lungs after surgery. This paper pools data from 99 patients in three clinical trials to set updated benchmarks for how long these patients live and how long they stay free of further events. The main finding is that outcomes vary widely, so the estimates remain about as uncertain as in earlier published work, and only the timing of the first recurrence (within two years of diagnosis) was clearly linked to a higher risk of an event.
summary.why: Lung-only recurrence after surgery is a group where new treatments might have the most impact, so reliable benchmarks matter for judging future trials. The authors argue that single-arm trials can only detect large effects in this setting and that smaller effects would need randomized comparisons; this is their reasoning from the data, not a settled consensus.

papers.abstract: ObjectiveOsteosarcoma is a rare primary bone cancer of adolescents and young adults without significant improvement in treatments or outcomes in several decades. Resection is standard of care for recurrent disease. Patients with lung only osteosarcoma recurrence following surgical resection (LOOR-FSR) may present the most meaningful opportunity for impactful intervention but alternative trial endpoints to objective response are needed. Here we update benchmarks for LOOR-FSR with contemporary clinical trial data. Patients/MethodsThis study included patients with pathologically confirmed LOOR-FSR enrolled on three Childrens Oncology Group phase 2 single arm trials. Benchmark endpoints assessed in this patient population were event-free survival (EFS) and overall survival (OS). In addition, we evaluated the impact of demographics and baseline clinical factors on outcome. ResultsNinety-nine patients met criteria for inclusion in this analysis. Median EFS and OS were 4.8 (95% CI: 3.5, 6.3) and 26.2 (23.3, 56.8) months respectively. Twelve-month EFS was 22% (15-31%) and ranged from 14% to 29% across the 3 trials, a difference that did not achieve statistical significance. The risk of EFS event was higher for those whose first recurrence occurred within two years of diagnosis (p=0.009). Other demographic and clinical factors did not statistically impact risk of event though estimated EFS for males was lower than for females. ConclusionDespite almost doubling the number of patients in this historical control cohort, wide variance in outcomes led to confidence intervals unchanged from previously published work. Until the most significant factors contributing to variability of outcomes in this patient population are quantified, single arm trials of new approaches will only be able to identify large effect sizes. Smaller effect sizes will require randomization.

papers.title: FlahyRecovery is an AI & gene expression based immune profiling biomarker for decision support in precision oncology
papers.label: medRxiv doi:10.64898/2026.11.12.26367994 v1

summary.background:
- Tumor microenvironment: the mix of immune cells, blood vessels, and supporting tissue surrounding a tumor.
- "Hot" vs "cold" tumors: informal labels for tumors with many versus few immune cells inside them. Cold tumors often resist immunotherapy.
- Immunotherapy: treatments that boost the body's own immune system to attack cancer.
- Gene expression: a measure of how actively each gene is being used in a tissue sample, usually obtained by sequencing.
- Supervised machine learning: a model trained on examples with known labels, then used to label new cases.
- Sensitivity and specificity: the share of true cases the model catches, and the share of non-cases it correctly rules out.
- AUC (area under curve): a 0 to 1 score of how well a model separates classes; 0.5 is chance, 1 is perfect.
- Validation cohort: a separate group of patients used to test the model after it was built.
summary.one_liner: A machine-learning classifier built on a 1,275-gene immune-signaling panel sorts tumor gene-expression profiles into Hot, Cold, or Intermediate immune subtypes, with reported links to survival and immunotherapy response in a multi-cancer validation cohort.
summary.plain: Tumors contain immune cells that can either attack cancer or be shut out of it, and doctors want to know which situation a patient's tumor is in before choosing treatment. This paper describes a computer model that reads the activity levels of about 1,275 immune-related genes in a tumor sample and sorts the tumor into one of three immune groups: "hot" (immune cells active), "cold" (immune cells kept out), or "intermediate." In a validation set of 1,337 tumors, the authors report the model agreed with the labels reasonably well and that "hot" tumors tended to have longer survival and better response to immunotherapy.
summary.why: Sorting tumors by immune activity could help decide who might benefit from immunotherapy and who may need combination treatment, which is a practical clinical question. However, the text is a short abstract and gives little detail on how the labels were assigned, how the model was tested, or how it would perform on independent patient groups, so its clinical value is not yet established.

papers.abstract: BackgroundAccurate characterization of the tumor microenvironment (TME) is crucial for inferring tumor biology, subsequent tumor behavior, and predicting therapeutic response. Current characterization methods are inadequate in capturing the complexity of immune signaling networks, hindering robust clinical decision making. To address this, we have developed FlahyRecovery - an artificial intelligence (AI) and gene expression based immune profiling biomarker, implemented via a supervised classification machine learning model, that integrates response prediction and prognostic insights to personalize treatment design, particularly immunotherapy. MethodsGene expression data of 7424 tumor specimens across 14 cancers was annotated specimen wise into three immune subtypes: Elevated Immunity (Hot) with high cytotoxic T-cell infiltration, Suppressed Immunity (Cold) marked by immune exclusion and stromal dominance, and Moderate Immunity (Intermediate) exhibiting mixed features. Following annotation validation, an AI model was trained and tested on the annotated data to classify new tumor specimens into the three immune subtypes - Elevated Immunity (Hot), Suppressed Immunity (Cold) and Moderate Immunity (Intermediate) based on the expression of a panel of 1275 genes involved in immune cell signaling and immune signal transduction. ResultsIn a multi-tumor validation cohort (N=1337), the subtyping model showed a sensitivity of 79%, a specificity of 89%, and a one-vs-rest AUC of 0.93. Elevated Immunity tumors correlated with prolonged survival and immunotherapy response, while Suppressed Immunity tumors correlated with treatment resistance and need for combination therapy. ConclusionArtificial intelligence can be effectively used to process tumor biology digitized via next-generation sequencing, to accurately mark the TME from an immunological perspective. Its clinical utility mechanisms andying patients who can benefit from immunotherapies, identifying treatment resistance mechanisms, and informing combination treatment regimes.
